projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lonnie Harland Boyett was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Good morning, Mr. Boyett, how are you doing today?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: About to settle down.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: About to settle down, all right. What branch of the military were you in?

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: What branch of the military were you in?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: I was a 2nd Armored Division, 82nd Army Recognizant Battalion, Headquarters Division.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: I volunteered.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Lacey Springs, Alabama.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Why did you join? Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Well, me and a guy got talking about it, you know, and I was a little old bitty guy, and they says -- I said -- they won't take you in, said you only weigh about 125, 130 pounds; said they won't take you in. So this guy, Harley Thomas, run a little grocery store down there, and he says, if you take it in, I'll set everybody up with a coke. So I went in and did all right, you know. I made corporal in 45 days. So anyhow, I went and got my little uniform after basic training, went back in, and I went down there, and Coke's were five cents a piece. So about four or five guys in there. I said okay, Harley, Harley Thomas is his name, I said, set them all up. He said, man, you're going to break me, said there are four or five guys in here. But anyhow, that's --

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Why did you pick the branch of the service you were in?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Well, I -- always my brother and them talking about a pension, you know, Army, Army, Army. So, you know, back in those days, there was no social security, all right, so I said, well, the Army's got a pension, so that's why, you know.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: I was --

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: I was called first days?

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Do you recall them?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah, sure. I was -- me and this guy, we went to -- down to re-enlist, you know, of course and he says well, let's join the Army, and I said, well, I'm too young, I said, I'll probably have to up my age. So I said, well, I'll just tell them -- I said I got my mom and dad to sign for me. So anyway, I said I'll tell them I was born in 1919, so I did. And it's on the record there 1919. So we went in, signed me up, they looked me over pretty close, because I was a little old bitty guy, weighed about 125 or 30 pounds, you know. And they looked me up and down, said -- and I -- physical, I passed it good, because I was a country boy, you know, and all that kind of stuff. So anyhow, they passed me, passed me on in, and I went in and did really good. In fact, I made corporal in 45 days, they said.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Tell me about your boot camp and training experiences.

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Yeah, it is Fort Benning, Georgia. Yeah, and I went in and really did -- really did good. They had these little campaign hats, you know, so the M1 rifle, you had to really get -- put it around back. So anyway, I went through boot camp; great, everything went great down in Fort Benning Georgia, yeah.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Do you remember your instructor?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: What now?

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Your instructor, or the Sergeant?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Sergeant Bennett, Sergeant Bennett was one. That's the only one I can remember.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: How did you get through your boot camp, did anything help you?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: No, no one helped me. I was a little rascal, I could -- you know, I could, you know, I could run, I could do anything. You know, I was in really good shape. I -- you know, really good shape and everything, so I had no problem getting through, you know.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: What wars did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: What awards?

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: What wars?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Oh, great goodness. I have -- should have brought my uniform along. I guess I'm about the only -- very few people have got the Star and Infantry badge, you know. That means two times being in combat, and in 2nd Armored Division, and we was Infantry, passed the Infantry Unit, and I got the Infantry Badge, you know. And another time I was in the infantry thing, and I got a Star and Infantry badge. My son-in-law, he retired as Major General, and he said that's something to be proud of, that Star and Infantry badge, you know.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: While you were in the military, where all did you go?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Where all did I go?

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Oh, great goodness. We went to -- when I joined, we, of course, went through basic training and all that kind of stuff, went on maneuvers in North Carolina, and we went to Fort Bragg, North Carolina, went on maneuvers there, and we had to swim across Mauks Lake -- Malt Lake. So I was so small and everything, they took pity on me, they put me on the other side helping those guys out, see. So anyway, when we left there, we went on the train to -- to -- where was that at now? Yeah, we went to -- up in New Jersey to do our vehicles, you know, to waterproof them all up at Camp Greg, New Jersey, and we waterproofed all the vehicles to go across, see.

So we went up to -- I went on invasion of -- went into Omaha Beach about two o'clock in the afternoon, and a beach here was about -- oh, about four or five miles around, you know. And this Captain that I almost passed out, he got killed, he went up -- he was a West Point graduate, Captain Bailey. Well, he went up on to Colonel, he obtained Commander. He had brought -- they was hauling those guys in that was killed on the beach, and I walked -- our landing craft, I walked in water about this deep (indicating), went on the beach.

So anyway, the grave Russian people was coming out and Colonel Bailey fell over like that and his eyes were (indicating), I liked to passed out. Because at Fort -- up at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, all the company commanders, he was a Captain then, had to learn how to ride a motorcycle, you know, because they may have to carry a message somewhere, you know. So he -- as I say he fell off, and his eyes like that, I liked to passed out, and he was a good friend of mine. But anyhow, up there riding a motorcycle, I come -- he said, this is the dog-gonish thing ever.

All I was trying to do is learn how to ride a motorcycle. He about six foot, six foot four inches tall and get on that motorcycle. He'd try to ride around to qualify. He said, well, how about just signing me, I said, well I can't do that, Captain, I said you got to learn how to ride this thing, because one of these days, you might have to ride it to carry a message. He said I know, I know, he said well, okay, he said -- but he finally learned, but he's the one that got killed, you know, and a good, good friend of mine, West Point graduate. Yeah.

But anyway, we went on and went on over at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. Went on to -- on the train and everything and we went on over up at, as I say, to waterproof our vehicles up at -- and I forget the name of the place now, I just mentioned it awhile ago there. And of course then we went on across to France -- I mean to Omaha Beach, you know. And then on through, all the way through.

And as I say, I rode a motorcycle and my motorcycle was shipped over and we got there, you know, and went on out. Funny thing -- this is a true thing. This old cow, I don't know how the old cow ever got through all the bombardment and things there was. Well, my corporal, he -- I told him, scout -- take a couple minutes, scout around down through there and see, because bullets was flying over and shells was going over, and all that kind of stuff. So this old cow must have been in a cave or something. So here come O' Hara running back down through there, and he said I seen the biggest German I ever wanted to see in my life, says -- so we went scouting on down down there, and it's this old cow. We laughed at O' Hara for the rest of the war.

But anyway -- but anyhow we went on through. And as I said say, I rode a motorcycle, I rode for George Patton a lot, and I was -- he was a mean guy, George Patton, General George Patton. I rode -- I escorted him for a lot, you know. And I really passed up a good deal with him, because he really took a liking to me. He was just a father figure to me, and he -- all general -- even One Star Generals -- he was a Major General, and them generals was -- and Battalion Commander was so scared, they'd come up out just trembling like that (indicating). But anyway, he really took a liking to me, because I escorted for him a lot.

My motorcycle, I had a 80 carburetor on it, and I'd get about 75 miles an hour and a Jeep could only get about 60 miles an hour, his Jeep, you know. So I could run ahead of him and everything, circle around, and all this kind of stuff. But anyhow, he was -- but all I had to do is just ask him, you know, to about battlefield promotions. Nobody made no promotions over there. All rank was froze. Nobody made no promotion in World War II. You went over there as a Private, you come back as a Private. I was a Buck Sargent all the way through.

Anyway, I had nine men, I was the 10th man riding a motorcycle, you know, and we escorted -- did a lot of escort duty plus messengers. And I had nine men, I was the 10th man, and we'd send out these messengers with messages, and I was the last man, you see, and a message come out, I'd have to carry it. Well, when I'd get back, usually they'd be gone, and we were going fast, you know, across over there, we were going -- and I'd come back. I would be lost, you know. I'd follow the tracks as far as I could, and I'd get lost.

I got a picture there in that medical outfit where I went in, someway or another got wounded and came in. But anyhow, I would go as far as I could, and then anyway, the story is that I was lost and I went in this town, I liberated this town. The Germans had been gone about two or three hours they said. Well, over there, these Germans would dress in American uniforms and turn our columns all around, you know. And I was a blond-headed, blue-eyed guy, strictly German look, you know, and everything. But anyhow, I went in this town and the Breugar Master, I convinced him I was American, you know.

Well, they put me down at the pub, you know, and the girls were kissing me all over, and I liberated. So anyhow, I was -- in the meantime, I lost -- this lady, I stopped, she give me some eggs, and I put them in my combat jacket here, see. So anyhow, about two o'clock in the morning, we was hipping it up in this cafe down there, and this guy come by, and seen my motorcycle sitting out there. So he come in there and got me, you know, put me on -- loaded my motorcycle up on the back of the Armor Reconnaissance Battalion car and carried me on in to my billywack area, you know, unloaded me.

So the next morning, I woke up and the German guys are back -- their back was to me. I started crying, I said, my goodness, I'm a German -- I'm American -- I'm a prisoner of the Germans, I said, my goodness. So my men comes through there with guns, so I jumped up, I had a head about like that, you know, from drinking that wine with those girls, you know. So I jumped up, and I ran through there, and started grabbing this ole' boy and started hugging him.

He said get away boy, I'm guarding these guys; you mean they're our prisoners; yeah, yeah, get away, get away. So anyway, I said, I said man -- that cured my head and everything, I said -- and aches was running down through here, and I was -- I had been lost about three or four days. So I said where's the medicine tent; he said right down there. So I went down there, and they all started laughing at me, and been down through here, and I had looked like I had -- the girls had been kissing me all over, you know, and I looked terrible.

They said man, you looked terrible, and they said man, you look terrible. I said, well I'm hungry as everything, said -- said well you got to go down there and clean up, said, a little bit, said take your shower down at the shower tent, and we'll have you new clothes and everything. So I did. And went back to the -- they me a stack of hotcakes about this tall, man, I eat like everything.

But anyhow, that was really -- but anyway, talking about this picture there where I had this -- I was lost again, of course, and I was carrying the ordnance report back, although I wasn't lost this time. I was carrying the ordnance report back, so they had a report out that a German guy was turning their columns all around, see, motorcycle riders, and they captured me in KiaZ, Belgium, captured me.

So they put me in this room with a -- took all my clothes off, it was cold and everything, I like to froze to death before they -- I tried to tell them I was an American guy, but anyway, they couldn't believe; yeah, yeah, yeah, we know you American citizen, said we got you, said we got you, said you've been turning our columns all around, said we got you.

I said well, man. I says send a message back to my outfit, I says. So they was scuffing me around pretty bad, so this Lieutenant walked in there, he said can't you see this man's a rebel, said he's from the south, said we're looking for a man from one of the England states. Said he's a rebel, says he's from the south; no. So, boy, they just about to hang me, that's all there was to it. They were just about to hang me.

They had been scuffing me around pretty bad. So anyway, they apologized to me, and then they did send a Morse Code message to my outfit, and I was given breakfast and everything. Well, it was about way up in the morning then, it wasn't even daylight, because it had been a couple of hours or something like that, maybe more, scuffing me around, and about to freeze to death. But anyhow, I went, got back to my outfit and everything. And there again, it was a rough, rough, rough road, a rough road. But anyway, I went all the way through the World War II riding that motorcycle.

And one little time I was in Tank D Company down in Fort Benning, Georgia, and I was in a tank for a little while. This Lieutenant got killed. These Lieutenants, they was -- boy, they didn't last too long, you know. But anyhow, they wanted me and this Colonel Johnson, he wanted me to take over this tank, oh, about four, five, six days in his tank, because I was in on D Company on maneuvers and all around. And Colonel Johnson he was -- he told me, says you get up there, and he says -- he gave me a bar, said I'll make you Lieutenant, said I'll put the paperwork through.

So my men, you know, said oh, man, said he shaved head, he'll get killed, seeing him wounded all the time, said man, you don't need to be in that tank, so I listened to them, you know, I listened to them, about three or four days. So this Lieutenant come from OCS and he come in there, and he told me, he says how about you let me ride that motorcycle, and you take and stay in this tank. I said no, Officer, I got to go back with my men. So he -- I rode about a day or two with him, and he took over the tank, you know, and that's the only time I was ever in the tank, you know. But anyhow, there's a lot of stuff I went through awhile, a lot of things I can't remember, you know, about the place, because I went -- as I say, all the married men come back first, and I was -- they had me pointed out for five points, so I was certain I wanted to marry then.

I come back -- I come back after, you know, after all the married men come back to the States. But anyhow, I tell you what, it's a lot of things. Guy asked me here awhile back, have you ever been shot at. And I don't know by the grace of the good Lord, that's why I'm here, I can't believe it. I can't believe it, because anyhow, me and some guys -- they had these little apple trees there and so me and some guy -- a couple of guys down looking at some apples, which we shouldn't have been, you know. But anyway, we didn't realize those Germans were probably an eighth of a mile down there.

So about -- several Germans, so they opened up on us. We start running like rabbits down through the grass about waist high, jumping. So, bullets are flying all around us, and I'll tell you, that's the truth, not a one hit us, not a one hit. There was three of us, and not a bullet hit none of us, and we run back down there and of course when they heard the shooting down there back up at our company, and they -- of course, they shot them. And here's the best one at all, my wife says why don't you tell this one, said you only have to tell one tale. So we were in this house, my men -- my motorcycle was sitting out there in this house.

And the guards are -- walked back and forth, and these SS troopers were leading these guys, and they are watching guards come, and when they'd come together, they'd slip on up, see, and they'd criss-crossing, the guards was, you see. So his house was there, and so this guy was slipping up, and he had his panaflo, it was like a potato masher, and it would penetrate -- it had penetrated our tanks, that panaflo would, like potato mashing, and they'd throw that thing, they could throw it some distance. But anyway, this guy was sleeping up at his house, and when I went out, I had to go to the restroom, we just go outside, you know, just go outside.

And I seen this -- well, I say we always carry -- we motorcycle riders had Tommy guns. So anyway, I see this helmet, you know, German helmets had a dip in the helmets, so I just fell back like that, and the moon shining, it come through a cloud, so I just fell back like that, and I pulled that Tommy gun around like that, and I opened up, and I cut him down like -- man like everything. When I did that, our men had about nine or ten -- I think there's a couple of other guys in with my men.

I had nine men, and they come out windows, doors, and every hole you can imagine when they heard that shooting, and the company was back over here (indicating), you know, like that, and they come out. And of course back down there, it was about, I guess probably about 30 or 40 Germans, and they were led by these SS troopers, see, SS troopers, and man they was -- that was German's best. But we opened up, and I guess we captured about 20 probably and killed about 30, you know, and I didn't -- I was running around trying to get my men there to get them organized, you know, and they was running, they were trying to bunch up, and I was trying to get them -- I didn't even shoot another shot.

I probably had shot all mine up, because of a six round I think we had a clip in it. But anyhow, I was trying to run around, trying to get these guys lined up, but them Germans, they were shooting like everything, too. And I don't even know how many, some -- I think about three or four of our men of the whole company, of course, they were back over there and they come in shooting and everything like that, and we was in between our company and the Germans, see. But that guy, I was supposed to get award out of that, but we were moving so fast, you know, but if he had got that window and throwed that panaflo in there, it would have killed every one of them or wounded them or concussion -- probably killed them all, but you know -- but anyway, that was the main one I was going to tell, and my wife says that was the best one at all, you know, and there was a window about this tall (indicating), and they knew that.

See, the Germans knew that, but they didn't -- our intelligence didn't know that these people was down there, because we were moving so fast, and we come into this place, you see, and we didn't know that they was congregated down there. And another time, we -- they had this Polish prison camp, the Germans did. And of course, I was -- I don't know where I was coming from, but they was working up on this road and they had these older German's guarding them, and I was on -- I was kicking on about 70 miles an hour, and I passed these guys working on the side of the road, they were Germans, see.

Well, since German guys was dressed like us, turned our columns around, they didn't pay much attention to me. See these old guys, older Germans were guarding these Polish prisoners, you know. Well, when I got back down there, the tanks was running through the fences, our tanks was, running through the fences, and those guys, there are probably 2 or 300 in that camp that were Polish prisoners or German prisoners, you know, people that they had got out of Poland and all. Anyway, they was running in every direction, running every direction, those guys was, and I seen one eat a chicken head, raw chicken head, and they fed them in a troft like that.

And they fed them, they pulled the soup in up here, and there was so much running down, you know, and the other soup would run on down. And those guys, they go in the fly by eating stuff like this, and they would have fly all over their face. Well they'd run all out in the countryside, you know, so we had to go out and gather them all up, and they are fighting, and families and the German families, you know, in these houses all around, and it took about two or three days to round all those Polish people up, get them back into camp, repair the fence. Of course they got them all, sent them all back, separated them out and put them on trains and everything like that and shipped them back to Poland, their homes, you know, took about four or five days for us all to get that done.

And it was quite a thing, quite a thing there; that all those Polish guys, you know, they was poor, bless their heart, was poor and everything, but the healthy ones, they was out there working, you know, but these -- but there was -- you'd go in these Germans houses, and they were about everything to the German people because they was all over the countryside there. But anyway, these -- it was quite a thing. As I say, I went all the way through World War II, went all the way. And met -- the Russian's, see, up river, we got there first, and we had to wait a couple, three days on the Russian's to come on the other side of the river, and the Germans were in there, and I was helping. We'd pull them out, you know, I had a Tommy gun.

But anyway, these guys were rivals, they'd reach down longer, pull the Germans out. And anyway, while we was waiting there, they had this crop duster, a German crop duster airplane, you know, and this guy, he was a pilot, and he -- we was taking our turns riding around. He said now, there's two sticks like this and the one in the middle was the one that carried you up, you know, you push it forward, and you pull it back, you go forward, and guide it like this, you know. He said do not touch that metal stick. He said you are in trouble if you touch that metal stick, says now just carry it, go left, go right, go left. Keep it straight so the field, you know, going in like that. So everybody said, all right, now your turn, now your turn.

I said oh, no, I don't fool with that thing, man; said oh, yes, said you got to. So I got in there, I took off around down through there, so I am going geh, geh, geh, geh, geh, geh, geh, geh, geh; said, you know what, said you was -- said back over there in the back, said you was waist high, said you was waist high off the ground; I said I never touched that middle stick; yeah, you must have touched that middle stick, because you was waist high off the ground, the wheels was; said you were fixing to go airborne; I said, said man, no, don't come on with that stuff; he said yes, said you were about to go airborne.

So I got so scared, I got so scared. I was safe back there, but I was about to pass out; said you were about to go airborne; all of them said yeah; I said look fellows, don't come here with that stuff; said yeah, you were -- but I like to have passed out. I never eat so much -- we captured this warehouse, the Germans had this -- sardines, I never eat so much hard crackers and sardines in my life.

But anyhow, that was that same place there where we were waiting on the Russian's to secure that place, you know, and we had ours, you know, that was the end of the war there. Them Russian's, they'd give you anything for a Mickey Mouse watch. Oh, man, they liked those Mickey Mouse watches. They would just have a fit over those Mickey Mouse watches. If they hadn't been paid, they were running out of a lot of money. They got paid, you know, I think, pretty soon, you know, because -- but they'd give you anything for a Mickey Mouse watch.

Great, goodness I tell you. But anyhow, there's all kind of story as I can say. You know, I just -- but many, many times I -- we'd take these towns and everything, and I'd go down to German -- get in his bed, they'd take off, you know, when we'd come in. But anyhow, we -- there was a lot of fun time, but it was -- all the time -- as I said, this guy asked me if I was shot at. Well, anyway, by the grace of the good Lord I'm here. You know, he -- if it wasn't for him, I -- if it wasn't for the good Lord, I wouldn't be here. My poor ole' mom, she prayed for me constantly. I could tell -- I could feel those prayers, I'll tell you. It was really --

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Praying you were messing with them apples, huh?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Over in Africa, you know, we -- the French landed in Casablanca, and I went all the way through Africa, go about 10,000 miles. And anyway, that picture there was took in Ramada, you know, and me and them guys was out looking for some oranges. They had the best oranges you'd ever taste. So these Arabs, in the morning they'd go by to bury their dead in the sunrise. You couldn't hardly see them. They'd move slowly across, slowly across, and they'd have little lock of hair up here that buried people sitting up, that feed that hair for 21 days. They'd guard it, they'd sit up there on them tumbleweed dressed in all that crap, they'd sit up there on the tumbleweeds, you couldn't even see them. So me and a couple of three guys, we were looking for oranges, see, in the orange grove.

We got down there. So this grave, you know, this red clay there, so all these Arabs do -- they just come out to bump us, knock us down, you know, and roll us over and stuff like that. So about four or five of them, maybe more than that, run out there and they'd just knock us down, they wouldn't try to hit us or nothing like that, but when we were down, they'd roll us over, we got all muddy and everything else. So we didn't get no oranges. But anyhow, we went back in the medic vac area, a place where -- and they said what in the world you guys been, we were all muddy; where in the world have you guys been; said y'all look terrible, said you guys look terrible. We were all muddy. We didn't get no oranges.

We found out that you couldn't -- they were sitting in those tumbleweeds, you know, and you couldn't tell, you couldn't tell. But boy, we were as close as that television, when we walked by some of them. But anyway it was crazy. Me and the guys, we had a lot of fun and everything else. But anyway, we tried to take one day at a time, you know, one day at a time. As I say, by grace of the good Lord, I'm here.

I had a good life back in the States, I had a good wife, run into a good one there. I was single; her, too and we've got 103 years between the marriages. We soon will be married seven years. She had been married 53 years to her husband, me over 50 years to my wife. So anyway, she got a very fine family. I mean the finest family. I got two great daughters, two just beautiful girls. And anyway, I love her family so much, so great. She got -- we're going this Sunday for one to be Christened, you know, a little girl, and so anyway at Frazier Memorial Baptist Church -- no, Methodist Church.

So anyway, we are very blessed, very blessed. We are both in pretty good health and all. I'm 87 years old, soon to be 88. And so I'm just really blessed, that's all. We go on trips, you know, and everything, and so we -- but I probably took more time --

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Oh you're good. We're good.

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: All your time up. So anyhow, as I say, she -- her granddaughter just had a little girl, and we -- it's kind of a -- well, it's really a neat thing. Her granddaughter, her kids Haley, Heather, and Hunter, and they named this little baby girl Hannah.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Hannah?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Yeah. So anyway -- but anyway, my children is -- I got a grandson. He's really doing well up in Claymore, Tennessee, and got all of them very well educated. My granddaughter got a Master's degree up in Huntsville. Her children, all her sons a CPA and other is a librarian, her oldest daughter is a librarian, two girls and a boy. And Linda, her middle girl, she's got two or three degrees. And my daughter, Mary Elizabeth two oldest daughter's a school teacher, which she don't have to teach no school, her husband's a Major General.

And anyway, and the youngest daughter, Linda, she's a banker. She's -- was -- she got -- finished college over at -- but anyhow -- at Troy, yeah. Well she got -- I don't know events or whatever, she's in the banking business. She an accountant over in Birmingham there.

But anyhow, and my grandson, Kevin, he's up in the money, he's up in the money. His wife is Holly, she makes commercial, you know, she makes commercials, and she got -- she -- they have a little boy and she got a little four year old boy, little Greg. So every one of our children is doing really good, and they're really good.

As I say, we're really blessed. I was single almost five years, and I prayed. I sat out there in my place, and I prayed, Lord, send me somebody to spend the rest of my life with. And I couldn't have found nobody better than this old girl right there. She was -- her husband died about a month after my wife died. So she was -- she has so much friends, though.

She goes all the time pretty much with this girl, Shirley, you know, she got this time sharing thing. But I just come from Jasper from my sisters. I got two sisters that live up there. And I'd go -- my sister, got two sisters that live up there, and I'd go -- my sister told me says you get out on 78, boy, you better watch it, because see, they're crazy, and she wouldn't lie. My goodness, I pulled out on that 78 from Jasper to Birmingham, and I tell you what, I run 70, and 80, and then with guys passing me, and I said I'll tell you, I can't believe this. Anyway -- but anyhow, my sister said please call me now, Lonnie, when you get home, because I want to see if you got there safe, and I did, I called her. But anyway, as I say, I'm really blessed on things. I got some tapes there.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Did the time you spent overseas in the war, has it affected the way you feel about life now?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: The time you spent in war, has it had an affect on the way you think about life now?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: Realize how blessed you are, huh?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I reckon so. Yeah, yeah, I'm not bragging. I'm not bragging, but I can tell you, my wife can tell you -- well, I don't know if I should say it or not --

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: You can brag, it's okay.

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: This lady -- well, not one, but stood outside my door, you know, and I'd look out there, and I'd be -- I'd see her, well, I was over at Collins, I just wanted to come over and check you out. So every time she sees my wife there, she says well, how are you all doing, how are you all doing. But anyhow, I know I'm not no Romeo, but I'll tell you what, I sure was blessed running into her.

I thought it wasn't even what I -- I told the good Lord, I said Lord, I'm sure there's somebody out there for me, but when -- you know, it's whooping up pretty close on five years, and I said I'll tell you what, I don't know. I run into these women, you know, and they like dogs and cats in their house, and we don't like -- we like animals, we like animals, but you know, we don't like dogs and cats all in our house, you know, slobbering all around.

Y'all might love them, but we like them, we like them. But we like them outside, you know. But anyway, as I say, I've been so blessed, and as far as I know, I'm in pretty good health and everything, and I'm looking forward to that flight on the 27th of May, and so -- to go to the World War II memorial and Korean War. Over in Korea, I was sitting up on the Mashiro border when the Chinese came across.

The OP, he looked -- got climbed up on the place, and he looked over there, and he said I've never seen in my life as many people in my life. The Chinese was -- before they come across -- see, we had North Korea took y'all on that. At one time we landed in China, I landed in China up in North Korea, and we swung north. And of course, as I said, we had North Korea took before the Chinese come across it, I was sitting on the Mashiro border, and I'll show you how blessed I was. My outfit went up -- I stayed up about 24 hours and come about a mile or two miles back, and stayed, I think, 48 hours, something like that.

Went up and when the Chinese come across. Well, the crew was up there, and I was the next crew to go up. The crew was up there, they said they melted the guns down, they melted the guns down shooting at those Chinese come across, you know, when they come across. Because they said you can -- Chinese, you can march twenty years, they marched 20 years 6 abreast and you never can kill them all. That's a true fact. They march 6 abreast for 20 years, you never can kill them, because younger ones growing on up fill the position. But this --

sp.speaker: Rachael Bernier
sp.p: They're on our side, though, right?

sp.speaker: Lonnie Harland Boyett
sp.p: The Lieutenant said, he never seen that amount of people in his life. As far as the human eye can see right and left they were assembling, he said. OP is observation post. But anyway, we had to march back down and when we went up, they said carry a fork, and we dropped our pack, it's probably five miles across, you know, we walked up. They said just carry your fork along, so we did.

And when we went back, we had to -- when the Chinese come across, we had to go back, see, walk because big Mosurt We climbed up on. So anyway, so I pick up my pack, as we went back, believe it or not, I picked up my pack with all the thousands of packs across there, and I got on the big -- but more opened it up. We hadn't shaved and everything, you know. Of course hadn't took a shower or anything when we shed our clothes, when we climbed up on the side, this rope stuff about ten guys climbed up at a time, big landing craft was going around like that to bring us in. When a guy falled off, they couldn't stop, they couldn't stop. He was just lost, because the landing craft, see, come right beside, and you climb up and we went right on the ship down to Pusan.

Of course, we started back up at 38 parallel. Well, those World War II Veterans, they were pretty much calling us out, because they called us out for being lunatics, I guess, because I was really out of it, I tell you what, I surely was. But anyway, I was in my 30s, I guess. Yeah, 32, 33, 34 years old. So anyway, I was an old guy then, see, old guy. I thought I never would get to 40. But anyway, when I got to 40, I says, I didn't have to take the PET course, I said I'll never make it, I'll never make it to 40. But anyway, I made it to two times 40 plus half a dozen plus. But anyhow, 87 years old, soon to be 88.

But anyhow, over my career, that was really something. I still lacked about three months. Went back to Japan and on a waiver, six months waiver, so they put me stock control, and I went to supply school. And Major Mims, I never shall forget him, he said can you make me a good man here, and you'll see, I'll sign you won't go back to Korea. I said Major, you have never seen what a good man I'll make you.

So in stock control, I had from 3 to 11, the Japanese, had about 40, I guess, stock, taking care of all the paperwork, Korea and all that. So anyhow, my shift was 3 to 11. And I was on this six months extension. So anyhow, Major assigned me to make me permanent. So anyway, I made really good there in stock control.

Those Japanese, they ate at six o'clock, and I'd go over at five o'clock and eat, that's when our -- they'd take out rice, and they'd chop it and they'd take it when it get -- they could drink that stuff, they'd drink that stuff, and have a fish head, see, fish head there, and they'd take that chop stick, hit that fish head, eye, pop it out. I tell you. I had a little balcony there, I'd walk out on that balcony, man, I tell you, I couldn't take that stuff.

All these girls, mostly girls -- it was an old man, Mr. Hat. He was an old retired Colonel. He didn't want to be called -- he only wanted to be called Mr. Hat. He was in China, missionary. But anyway, we was -- I worked there for -- before it went in the management branch. He wanted me to help him, or like this. We both smoked Roman Maple, smoked a pipe. I still got my pipe, it was in my pack, believe it or not. But anyway, me and Mr. Hat, he taught me so much about management, you know.

And anyway, this guy down in central receiving section, he wanted me -- he said he wanted me to come down there. I don't know, I guess I did a good job in stock control, and he requested me to come down to central receiving section. So, of course I went down there, because he was civilian, but he was pretty ranking guy, you know, he was about a GS-12 or something like that, made by a Major or Colonel. But anyway, went down, he was from Hyaloid and he was a fine fellow.

Me and him got along great, and we had these big -- when they confiscated the Japanese, they got these over and under pistols and all kinds of various stuff, and it was in a room almost big as this with three locks, me and him was the only two. These guys would come around dressed as privates and all, they was colonel's and CID guys, you know, CID is like FBI on the outside, and they'd come around and try to con us. You know, here's a thousand dollars bill, I know you can get in there, and I'd like to have an over and under pistol, said I'll give you thousand dollars.

You're probably a Colonel, see dressed as a POC or a Private, anyway. So a lot of time, I look at that thousand dollar bill, see, and man, I'd almost get that key and go out there and start to unlock it. But good Lord told me boy, up in watch shop, the guy up there, with these flying watches he polished 125 dollars they'd cost.

Because, you know, high flying pilots, they cost 125 dollars, they got this guy up there. He sold -- he bought -- they bought one or two from him, and the last time out, he was out in Company arrest in the Barricks Company. I don't know what happened to him, I left. But anyway, that central receiving section, I really had it made.

We had about twenty, twenty Polish girls, you know, and Johnny was my interpreter. He could speak good English, and I'd carry on with those people. Over at production control, these tanks over there was -- that come from Korea shot up, and they'd fix them in old production control. So anyway, I was in charge of it, too.

But anyhow, Johnny, I'd get talking to him Japanese, hut, hut, hut, hut, he'd carry on, he'd laugh. He'd laugh so much that all them little ole' Japanese girls, they'd get back out of there and giggle and everything, and I'd carry on like crazy. But anyway, I was kind of a comical guy anyway around with them. But anyhow, Rita had made it over there, and my wife come over there, my youngest daughter, they almost buried her at sea, she had convulsions, Linda.

They gave me a staff card to go down to Oklahoma and pick my wife and girls up. So anyhow, out on the -- they'd see me down there and they'd spot their husband down there, honey, honey, honey; I thought they were saying Lonnie, Lonnie; and I'd yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, it wasn't me, I thought it was my wife, you know. But anyhow, yeah, yeah, yeah. But anyhow, they give my wife the Captain's quarters with my daughter, Linda.

She had these convulsions, and she almost died, and they had permission to bury her at sea. But anyway, I thought -- but she come off, they brought her off, you know, separate and everything. So anyway, over in Japan, I had good, nice quarters, a maid, and all that stuff, you know, good stuff, yard boy and all. So anyway, we carried them.

So this ole' boy, Coal Blazer, he was a mean guy, had his Ford convertible down Tokyo there, he'd -- these women go around with stuff on their head, and he'd go with a Coal Blazer, he'd knock them off, so they'd put him in jail and confiscate his car, his Ford convertible. So anyway, I went down there and signed for him to get out, you know, and so I had his car, and so I told my wife and everything when we got out there to her quarters, I says over here, we just pick out a car that we like. I said I like that ole' blue convertible, you know, I said, let's go out there and get it.

I said I bet the keys are in the glove compartment, which I know there was, because I had put them there. So I got in, the girls jumped in the back, they were four or five years old. So they jumped in the back; yeah, yeah, yeah. So we was going down to eat, you know, at the drive-in and Lois, my wife, said get out of there, you're going to get in trouble.

First off, we just got over here and you're going to get in trouble, said, stealing a car. I said I'll tell you what, if the keys are in the glove compartment, then we got it. So I said oh, yeah, yeah, all right. See the keys are right there. I said, heck, come on, let's go, let's go. So we went down there. I was so excited and I ran over the curb. I wasn't used to driving. I run over the curb. But anyway, we -- of course we went back and my wife got talking to the maid and all that kind of stuff.

So we got settled down and everything, and it was in a the R041B is right in the backyard porch, and drive all around like that and the parking lot was out here. And we had the little girls would ride, the tykes, the bicycles around, you know. So Linda, my youngest daughter, she'd stand on the back and my oldest daughter, Mary Elizabeth, she would ride around.

So right over on the corner, this guy's wife, a big ole' redheaded women, all the women were pretty scared of her, see. Patricia was six years old, and said she'd hold her arms out like this, she wouldn't let them pass, okay. So I had come in that night, oh, the kids are crying; Lois, my wife, yeah, they running, little ole' Patricia won't let them pass. So I got down on my knees, this might not be right, Mary Elizabeth, she was a pretty strong little girl, she was five years old, I said honey, I tell you what, now you make like this is Patricia's face, just take your little fist now, I said, you just make like this is Patricia's face, and you just pop, pop, pop, pop, pop. When she stops like that, you get off your little trike, tricycle, and go right around them, and I said, you just get -- you make like this, her face now, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop.

So I trained about two or three a week, something like that. So same thing. Patricia held her arms out like Mary Elizabeth, held them out, then run plumb in the house, this big ole' red-headed woman, Mary Elizabeth hit Patricia. All the women, four, five, three women, four women, Lois, my wife, was there, so they was all looking, so they knew what was going to happen, see. Lois passed the word around, my wife passed the word around what was going to happen. So they was so tickled. They was so tickled about -- they had a ball.

I went in that night and all of them was over at my apartment or quarters, and I went in and I thought, I thought, boy, they was having a party. Man I tell you, blinds was down and all like that. And Mary Elizabeth, she had done -- she was king of the walk, she was king of the walk. Patricia never no more stopped them like that. Mary Elizabeth, she was the king of the walk.

This was up in Fort Knox, Kentucky. I was a gunner on the 105 Houser, and we'd shooting over the OCS, the OCS, the cadets is -- we shooting an L, firing an L, and I had the center gun here. I was the one setting the sites and firing. We were shooting over these the OCS cadets there, OP6, so I just froze, I froze like this. And Major Gouch -- Lieutenant, fire, fire, fire.

Well, you know, when the firing does it, up, up, up I couldn't tell, so I -- he come up there and said uh, he said man, said you pushed that lantern, said you know where we'd hit. I said well, I didn't know where we'd hit, but I says the good Lord just told me. I've always kind of -- I've always been a pretty religious guy, you know, all the time. Anyhow, he said you'd hit right in the middle of OP6. I like to passed out. I said man, what are you talking about? He said that's right. Said I went the wrong way with my sights, see, and I put the gun, you know, a certain degree.

So he said man, he said cut that thing down. So I did. Anyway, we went on and we went overseas over in Japan, so we were down to the theater, and he had made captain, he was First Lieutenant. Anyway, he was at the theater down there, somebody tapped me on the shoulder, and looked down, it was him, he was a captain. I said man, I said, you are looking very good. He said you are coming up a little bit, too, I said yeah, I said, well, look a big eight ball here.

I said you want two big eight balls, I tell you what, if you push that lantern, said we'd be both in Fort -- underneath the prison. So anyhow, he was -- we met each other a lot, you know. And after that, come back from overseas, we was in this airplane, and this guy and his wife, we was on the outside, I had two girls and he had two girls. So we are flying back from Frankfort to Washington D.C., so we -- there's four engines, you know, and this one just cut off.

And I said, you know what, I said you see this dog gone thing here, it's cut off. He said hell, you say; I said yeah, look yonder, we better tell somebody about this, I said. So the hostess come by and she was Lieutenant, I said look here, this dog gone thing stopped, this motor stopped over there.

She says -- kind of laughed, she said yeah, I know. I said well, look here, you better tell the guy operating this thing about this. She said well, I'll tell him. She went on not too concerned, and I told this guy, I said, you know, I said she don't take this thing serious, man, said that thing's stopped, said we are out in the middle of the ocean; yeah, I know. She said well, I'll tell you what's happening, I said tell me, girl. So she says, we had to change -- have to cut your motor off to change your tanks. Said instead of keeping it fired up, said we'll get it to start a fire, so we had to cut the motor off, so we do that so you'll see, again, says as we go along, have to cut the motor off to change tanks, you know.

So anyway, we -- that was -- I pretty scared there on that, you know. But anyway, we -- on the ship when we first started Sergeant Brooks, I never will forget him. He said I'll tell what you to do, he said right on the top of your duffle bag, be sure you put a clipboard, and then a mark far across it. And said you can go all over the ship, the other guys keep them from fighting and everything, you know, and chipping paint all the time, chipping paint. So anyway, I'd walk around on the ship with my clipboard, you know, fire across there, and the guy would say how did you get that detailed, man.

I said well, you got to know somebody; well, who do you know. Anyway, I went over twice on a ship, first on the British ship, eat so much billy goats, I don't want to think about it. But anyway, I walked around on that ship, you know, and guys be smoking, you know, they smoking out on the ship, and cigarette go in the porthole and set the ship a fire. Anyway, I see them smoking, well, I didn't have but a bit more authority than they did, but I had my clipboard in my arms and coming back. My wife and everything come on the ship, see, so they was up above us and we'd slip underneath.

But I was right up the front line eating breakfast and every meal, you know, they'd say how in the world do you do that; I said well, this is how I got this, I said I'm fire guard; fire guard; yes, I'm a fire guard. But anyway, but I was in the first line, and these women -- these women be -- they'd be coming back and going over, and see, the teachers know all that, and they would -- they would -- they'd be up there sunbathing, and all that kind of stuff, and I'd walk around up there.

I'd be up there with that captain, this big thing there, you know, the ship keeping it on course. I was up with him, you know, and that kind of stuff. But anyway, I was -- I always was pretty blessed on all things, you know. A lot of things, I don't remember, but some things -- I know I jumped around, and everything, but when you get my age, hey, you can't think of everything.

But I tell you what, I'm just really blessed, really blessed on it all. So anyway, that's about my story. I brought a gang of tapes along, but those I want to keep to give to my girls and, as time goes on, you know. I'll tell you what, I'm planning on living to 100 years old.

Yeah, I told my son-in-law, I said now, when I get 90 years old, I want a big party. I want a big party when I get 90 years old. But anyway, I know I probably took more time than I should, but anyhow, that's pretty much my story.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
